title: The Way You Do Things
description: Everyday habits, routines, and your own ways of getting things done.

questions.text: When you need to focus, what do you usually do to get started?

steps: Describe what you do first.
Explain how it helps you begin.
responseGuide.example: I put my phone in another room and open only what I need. That makes it easier to start without checking messages.

observe: How the learner makes an everyday method clear with a concrete detail.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Think about the last time you had too much to do. How did you decide what to do first?

steps: Set the scene briefly.
Explain what you chose first and why.
responseGuide.example: Yesterday I had several small tasks waiting. I started with the quickest one because finishing something helped me get going.

observe: How the learner gives enough context to understand one specific event.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: What is one everyday thing you do your own way, and why?

steps: Choose one everyday activity.
Explain your method and why it works for you.
responseGuide.example: I lay out everything I need before making breakfast. It takes a minute, but I do not have to keep opening cupboards.

observe: How the learner connects a choice or method to their stated reason.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a time someone suggested a different way to do something.
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: Think of an ordinary moment, such as making, fixing, or organizing something.

steps: Say what you were doing.
Recall their suggestion and your response.
responseGuide.example: I was sorting some photos when someone suggested making folders by year. I said I usually sorted them by event. They showed me their system, but I kept mine because it was familiar.

observe: How the learner distinguishes what each person said or meant.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Think about the last time you looked for something you couldn’t find. What did you do?
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: It can be something small you misplaced at home.

steps: Say what you were looking for and where you started.
Describe what you tried next and how the search ended.
responseGuide.example: I could not find a note I had written. First I checked my bag, then I looked through the papers on my table. I still did not find it, so I stopped looking for a while.

observe: How the learner connects the main events in a clear sequence.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Think about a recent change to your routine. How did you react?

steps: Describe the change briefly.
Explain your reaction with one detail.
responseGuide.example: My usual shop was closed, so I had to go somewhere else. At first I was annoyed, but finding a closer shop was useful.

observe: How the learner connects their stated reaction to what happened.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: What is one everyday habit you have changed over the years?

steps: Describe how you used to do it.
Explain what changed and how you do it now.
responseGuide.example: I used to keep every task in my head. Now I write a short list. I started doing that after forgetting something small but important.

observe: How the learner explains a change or a reason to keep doing something.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

title: Decisions & Why You Make Them
description: Everyday choices, changing your mind, and explaining your reasons.

questions.text: Tell me about a small decision you made recently that made your day easier.

steps: Name the decision.
Explain what became easier.
responseGuide.example: I decided to prepare lunch before starting a long task. Later, I could take a proper break without wondering what to eat.

observe: How the learner gives enough context to understand one specific event.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: When someone invites you somewhere, what helps you decide whether to go?

steps: Describe what you consider.
Give one everyday example.
responseGuide.example: I think about how much time I have and whether I want company. If my day is already full, I sometimes suggest another time.

observe: How the learner connects a choice or method to their stated reason.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a decision you talked through with someone before making it.
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: A small everyday choice is enough; it does not need to be a major decision.

steps: Explain the choice briefly.
Recall what each of you said.
responseGuide.example: I was choosing between two activities. My friend asked which one I would still want to do next month. I said I liked different things about each one. We talked for a while, but I was still unsure.

observe: How the learner distinguishes what each person said or meant.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you heard something that made you rethink a decision.

steps: Explain what you had planned to do.
Describe what you heard and how it affected your thinking.
responseGuide.example: I was going to join an evening class. Then someone mentioned how much practice it involved outside class. I started wondering whether I had enough time. I have not decided yet.

observe: How the learner connects new information to their stated reaction or reconsideration, without requiring a final decision.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: When someone suggests doing something you haven’t tried before, how do you decide whether to give it a go?

steps: Describe what you want to know before deciding.
Use one example to explain what matters to you.
responseGuide.example: I usually ask what it involves and how long it takes. Someone recently suggested trying a board game. I said yes because we could play one short round and see how it went.

observe: How the learner makes their decision process understandable through a reason and a concrete example.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: When was the last time you changed your mind about something?

steps: Explain your first choice.
Describe what changed your mind.
responseGuide.example: I planned to stay home last weekend. Then I realized I had spent most of the week indoors, so I decided to take a short walk.

observe: How the learner explains a change or a reason to keep doing something.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Walk me through a recent decision that took longer than you expected.
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: Think of a choice you kept putting off or comparing options for.

steps: Introduce the choice.
Describe the main steps that led to your decision.
responseGuide.example: I wanted to choose a book. First I read a few descriptions, then I tried the opening pages. In the end, I picked the one I wanted to keep reading.

observe: How the learner connects the main events in a clear sequence.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

title: Conversations & People
description: What people say, how you respond, and how conversations unfold.

questions.text: Tell me about a recent conversation that lasted longer than you expected.
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: It could be a conversation in person, on the phone, or through messages.

steps: Say who you were talking to and how the conversation began.
Describe what kept you talking and how it ended.
responseGuide.example: I asked someone if they had finished a book I had lent them. They had, but we disagreed about the ending. We kept comparing different parts until I noticed how late it was.

observe: How the learner distinguishes what each person said or meant.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: What do you usually do when you do not understand what someone means?

steps: Describe how you respond.
Give an example of what you might say.
responseGuide.example: I repeat the part I understood and ask about the rest. I might say, “Do you mean today or next week?” That usually clears things up.

observe: How the learner makes an everyday method clear with a concrete detail.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Think about a time you misunderstood someone. How did the conversation unfold?
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: The misunderstanding does not need to have been resolved.

steps: Explain what you first thought they meant.
Describe what happened next, including anything that remained unclear.
responseGuide.example: Someone said they would call me later, and I thought they meant that evening. I waited, but they called the next day. We never discussed what “later” meant to each of us.

observe: How the learner connects the main events in a clear sequence.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: When you need someone’s help, how do you usually start the conversation?

steps: Give an example of how you would start.
Explain why you start that way.
responseGuide.example: I usually ask, “Have you got a minute?” Then I explain what I am trying to do. I start that way because the person might be busy, and I can ask later if needed.

observe: How the learner illustrates an opening and explains why they use it, without prescribing one culturally correct way to ask for help.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you explained a choice that someone did not understand.

steps: Introduce your choice briefly.
Recall how you explained your reason.
responseGuide.example: I chose to take a longer route. Someone asked why, so I explained that it was quieter and I had time. They understood once I gave that detail.

observe: How the learner gives enough context to understand one specific event.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Think about a recent conversation. Is there anything you would explain differently now?

steps: Choose one part of the conversation.
Explain what you would keep or change and why.
responseGuide.example: I explained a problem but spent too long on the background. Next time I would say what went wrong first, then add the detail that matters.

observe: How the learner explains a change or a reason to keep doing something.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a time someone said something that surprised you.

steps: Recall what they said.
Explain your reaction and response.
responseGuide.example: Someone told me they remembered a small favor from years ago. I had forgotten about it, so I was surprised. I said I was glad it had helped.

observe: How the learner connects their stated reaction to what happened.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

title: Things That Happened
description: Everyday stories, unexpected moments, and what happened next.

questions.text: Tell me about an ordinary day when something unexpected happened.
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: A small interruption or discovery is enough for a story.

steps: Set the scene in one sentence.
Walk through the main events in order.
responseGuide.example: I was tidying a drawer when I found an old note. I read it, remembered who wrote it, and sent that person a message. We had not spoken for a while.

observe: How the learner connects the main events in a clear sequence.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about something that made you laugh recently.

steps: Describe what happened or what someone said.
Explain what you found funny about it.
responseGuide.example: I was looking for my glasses when someone pointed out that I was wearing them. I had checked two rooms already. I laughed because I had been using them to look for themselves.

observe: How the learner gives enough context to understand their stated reaction, without judging whether the event is funny or labelling the learner.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a time you shared unexpected news with someone.
questions.supportPrompt: If you need help getting started: The news can be ordinary; you do not need to share anything private.

steps: Explain the news briefly.
Recall what you said and how they responded.
responseGuide.example: I found something we had been looking for. I sent a message saying where it was. The other person replied immediately and asked how I had found it.

observe: How the learner distinguishes what each person said or meant.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a recent plan that turned out differently from what you expected.

steps: Describe the original plan.
Explain what happened instead.
responseGuide.example: I planned to spend the afternoon outside, but it started raining. I stayed in and finished a book. The day was different, but I enjoyed it.

observe: How the learner gives enough context to understand one specific event.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: When something small goes wrong during your day, what do you usually do first?

steps: Describe your first step.
Give a small everyday example.
responseGuide.example: I pause to work out what actually happened. If I cannot find my keys, I check the last place I remember using them before looking everywhere.

observe: How the learner makes an everyday method clear with a concrete detail.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Tell me about a small mistake that changed how you do something now.

steps: Describe the mistake briefly.
Explain what you do differently now.
responseGuide.example: I once left a message unfinished and thought I had sent it. Now I check that important messages have actually gone through before putting my phone away.

observe: How the learner explains a change or a reason to keep doing something.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.

questions.text: Think about something you tried for the first time recently. Why did you try it?

steps: Say what you tried for the first time.
Explain what led you to try it.
responseGuide.example: I tried drawing a familiar object. I wanted a short break from screens, and all I needed was paper and a pencil. It was harder than I expected.

observe: How the learner connects a choice or method to their stated reason.
avoid: Do not demand a story for a question about habits or reasons. Do not invent motives, feelings, dialogue, or outcomes. Do not infer stable traits.
